sentences.asr: The charts present the findings of a survey on consumers' acceptance of elderly care robots and their primary concerns.
As the pie chart shows, 39.3% of the respondents fully accept these robots and another 32.8% accept them partially, while the remaining 27.9% reject them altogether.
Meanwhile the bar chart reveals that safety tops consumers' concerns at 46.3%, far ahead of price, 24.9%, and convenience, 10.7%.
Several factors may account for these figures.

On the one hand, as the population ages rapidly and professional caregivers are in short supply, more and more families regard robots as a practical way to care for elderly relatives, which explains why over 70% of consumers are open to them.
On the other hand, elderly people are physically fragile, so even a minor malfunction could cause serious harm.
Hence safety ranks first, and some consumers reject the robots altogether.
In my view, elderly care robots have a promising future, but their popularity depends on public trust.
Manufacturers should give top priority to safety and reliability, while the government ought to set strict standards and offer subsidies to make these products affordable.
Only in this way can technology truly bring comfort to our senior citizens.
The bar chart illustrates the results of a survey on people's views of children's outdoor activities.
As can be seen, satisfying curiosity and improving observational skills are the two most widely recognized benefits, chosen by 54.6% and 54.5% of the respondents respectively.
By contrast, building physical fitness and strengthening parent-child interaction were selected by only 37.2% and 33.2% respectively.
These figures indicate that people value outdoor activities mainly for their contribution to children's intellectual growth.
Nature offers children endless things to explore, which naturally sparks their curiosity and sharpens their powers of observation.
The relatively low percentages for health and family bonding, however suggest that some benefits of outdoor activities are still underestimated.
In my opinion, physical exercise and family time outdoors are just as vital to children's healthy development.

Therefore, schools should encourage children to spend more time outdoors, and parents should join them whenever possible, so that children grow up healthy, curious and closely connected with their families.
The table shows the average number of air conditioners, washing machines and refrigerators owned per 100 Chinese households at the end of selected years from 2014 to 2023.
The most striking change is in air conditioners, whose number nearly doubled from 75.2 to 145.9.
By comparison, ownership of washing machines and refrigerators grew more gradually, from 83.7 to 98.2 and from 85.5 to 103.4 respectively.
These figures clearly reflect the steady improvement in people's living standards.
With rising incomes, durable goods that were once luxuries have become everyday necessities.
Since most families already own a washing machine and a refrigerator, demand for them is approaching saturation.
Air conditioners, however are still spreading fast, because many households now install one in each room in pursuit of greater comfort.
In my view, this trend is encouraging, but it also brings new challenges.
More appliances mean higher energy consumption and more electronic waste.
Therefore, manufacturers should develop more energy-efficient products, and consumers should use them responsibly and recycle old ones properly.
Only in this way can a better life go hand in hand with a greener planet.
The bar chart presents the results of a survey on the main leisure activities of the elderly in a community.
Watching TV is by far the most popular, chosen by 90.8% of the respondents, followed by taking walks at 68.3%.
In contrast, growing flowers, reading and playing chess are much less common, at 34.7%, 31.8% and 18.4% respectively.
The chart suggests that most senior citizens prefer leisure activities that are easy and inexpensive, requiring no special skills or partners.
Television brings them news and entertainment at home, while walking is a simple way to keep fit.
Activities that demand more skill, concentration or company, such as reading and playing chess, attract far fewer people.
In my opinion, older people deserve a wider range of leisure activities.

Communities could organize reading clubs, gardening classes and chess competitions, which would not only make older residents' spare time more rewarding, but also help them stay mentally active and socially connected.
The picture and the chart reflect a pleasant change in urban life.
In the picture, residents are walking, jogging and exercising happily in a public fitness area. And a boy exclaims, the new little park near my home is wonderful.
The chart shows that the number of parks in a city rose steadily from 406 in 2020 to 532 in 2021, and then to 670 in 2022, an increase of about 65% in just two years.
The implied meaning is clear. More and more small parks are being built right on people's doorsteps, greatly improving the quality of their daily lives.
This trend results from both the government's commitment to people-centered urban planning and citizens' growing health awareness.
These pocket parks offer convenient places for exercise, relaxation and social contact, making cities greener and more livable.
In my view, this practice deserves wider promotion.
Planners should make full use of idle land to create more green spaces, while residents should take good care of these facilities.
After all, a city truly becomes a home when everyone can enjoy nature just a few steps away.
The chart shows what students at a university gained from their labor practice course.
Acquiring relevant knowledge tops the list at 91.3%, closely followed by improving practical skills at 84.8%.
Meanwhile, 54.4% of the students reported feeling happier and more relaxed, while only 32.6% believed their teamwork ability had improved.
These figures suggest that the course has achieved remarkable success.
By working with their own hands, students not only gain useful knowledge that textbooks cannot offer, but also become more competent in daily life.
Moreover, physical work serves as a good way to relieve academic stress.
However the low percentage for teamwork indicates that cooperation has not received enough attention.
In my opinion, labor education is an indispensable part of higher education.
Universities should continue to offer such courses and design more group tasks so that students can develop practical skills and a cooperative spirit at the same time.
As the picture shows, a dragon boat race is being held on a river in a village.
Several boats are speeding under a stone arch bridge, while crowds of villagers line both banks, cheering excitedly.
Watching the lively scene, an elderly couple smile and say, how wonderful.
The dragon boat race in our village is getting livelier every year.
The picture reflects the revival of traditional culture in rural China.
The dragon boat race, a custom with a history of over 2,000 years, is not only an exciting sport but also a symbol of teamwork and community spirit.
As rural living standards have risen, villagers now have both the means and the enthusiasm to celebrate their traditions.
Such festivities enrich their cultural life, strengthen the bonds among neighbors and even attract tourists, thereby boosting the local economy.
In my view, this trend deserves our applause.
Traditional customs are the roots of a nation and keep our shared memories alive.
Therefore we should support folk activities, encourage young people to take part in them and integrate them into rural revitalization efforts.
In this way, our traditions will not only survive but thrive, bringing new vitality to the countryside.
The line chart illustrates the changes in the health literacy level of Chinese residents from 2012 to 2021.
As the chart shows, the proportion of residents with basic health literacy rose year after year from 8.80% to 25.40%, nearly tripling.
Notably, the growth sped up from 2016 onward, with the figure more than doubling from 11.58% to 25.40% in just five years.
Several factors may account for this trend.
First with rising living standards, people are paying increasing attention to their health.
Second, the government has made great efforts to promote health education, especially since the Healthy China 2030 Plan was issued in 2016.
Third, the internet has made it much easier for people to obtain reliable health information.
In my opinion, this improvement is encouraging, yet there is still much room for progress, since about three quarters of residents lack basic health literacy.
Therefore health knowledge should be spread more widely, especially in rural areas, so that everyone can make wise decisions about their health.
Dear Professor Brown
I am writing on behalf of the Student Union to invite you to organize a team for the International Innovation Contest, which will be held at our university from May 10th to 15.
The contest aims to bring together young innovators from around the world to share creative ideas.
Each team of four to six students will present a project in a field such as clean energy.
Given your outstanding achievements in technological innovation, we would be honored if you could lead a team from your university.
Accommodation will be provided free of charge.
Please let us know by April 10th whether you can join us.
We look forward to your reply.
Sincerely yours, Li Ming.
As the pictures show, two students are standing in front of a poster for a campus lecture.
One of them is reluctant to attend, saying it's not related to our major, so it won't be of much use to us.
Her classmate, however replies, let's go and listen.
It's bound to do us good.
The pictures reveal two contrasting attitudes toward learning.
The first student holds a narrow, utilitarian view, valuing only knowledge directly related to her major.
By contrast, her classmate realizes that knowledge from other fields can broaden one's horizons and spark new ideas.
In fact, many breakthroughs come from the intersection of disciplines. For example, advances in biology now depend heavily on computer science.
Limiting ourselves to one field may seem efficient in the short term, but it restricts our potential in the long run.
As college students, we should be open-minded learners.
Instead of asking whether a lecture will pay off immediately, we should seize every opportunity to explore new areas, attend lectures across disciplines and read widely.
Only by doing so can we develop a well-rounded mind and meet the challenges of a rapidly changing world.
The bar chart illustrates the changes in China's express delivery volume from 2018 to 2020.
The total volume grew steadily from 51 billion parcels to 83 billion, an increase of about 63%.
Meanwhile, the rural volume rose even faster, from 12 billion to 30 billion, an increase of 150%.
As a result, its share of the total climbed from less than a quarter to over one-third.
Several factors contribute to this boom.
To begin with, online shopping has become part of daily life, generating a huge demand for parcel delivery.
In addition, improved rural roads and logistics networks now allow express services to reach remote villages.
Moreover, e-commerce helps farmers sell their produce across the country, which further boosts rural deliveries.
In my view, the rapid growth of express delivery, especially in the countryside, benefits both consumers and the economy.
However, billions of parcels also create mountains of packaging waste, so companies should switch to eco-friendly materials and encourage recycling.
In the picture, a little boy dressed in a Peking Opera costume says to his father, Dad many of my classmates think learning Peking Opera is no fun.
His father smiles and replies, You like it yourself. Don't you?
Then that's all that matters.
The picture conveys a simple yet profound message. We should follow our own interests rather than other people's opinions.
Many young people give up their hobbies simply because others consider these hobbies dull or old-fashioned.
However, it is genuine passion that keeps us going when we face difficulties and eventually leads us to success.
Moreover, the boy's love for Peking opera reminds us that traditional art needs young successors, and only those who truly love it can carry it forward.
In my view, the father sets a good example for all parents.
Parents should respect and support their children's genuine interests rather than push them to follow the crowd.
As young people, we should have the courage to stick to what we love, no matter what others say.
After all, a life driven by passion is far more rewarding than one shaped by other people's expectations.
The bar chart illustrates how residents of a city exercise.
As can be seen, exercising alone is the most popular way, chosen by 54.3% of the respondents, closely followed by exercising with friends at 47.7%.
By contrast, only 23.9% exercise with their family members, and group activities rank last at a mere 15.8%.
Several factors may account for this.
For one thing, exercising alone is flexible, as people can work out whenever they are free.
For another, friends usually share similar interests and habits, which makes it easy for them to exercise together.
Exercising with family or in groups, however is less common, probably because of busy schedules and a lack of organized activities in communities.
In my opinion, every way of exercising has its own advantages.
Whatever form people choose, what matters most is to make exercise a regular habit.
In addition, communities could organize more group activities, such as weekend fun runs and family sports days, to make exercise more enjoyable and sociable.
Dear Paul
I'm delighted that the letters moved you as much as they moved me.

They were written by ordinary Chinese families over the past century. Parents encouraging children studying far from home. Soldiers reassuring their loved ones from the front, and couples sharing news across long distances.
Faded as some of them are, they preserve genuine emotions and record the great changes of their times.
Yes, a large collection of these letters is now on public display in a family letter museum in Beijing, and admission is free.
If you come to China this summer, I'll gladly take you there and tell you the stories behind them.
Yours Li Ming
Dear Jack
Thank you so much for sharing the video of your family's trip in China.
I have watched it twice and enjoyed every minute of it.
The magnificent Great Wall, the bustling night markets and, above all, the happy smiles on your faces made me feel as if I were traveling with you.
It was truly heartwarming to see how much you love Chinese culture.
I'm eager to learn more about your journey.
Which city impressed you most? And what was your favorite local food?
I'd also love to hear any interesting stories that were not in the video.
I'm looking forward to your reply.
Best wishes. Li Ming.
Dear Paul
Thank you for your interest in the craft demonstration.
Next Friday afternoon, five young craftsmen will come to our campus to show how they breathe new life into traditional crafts.
For example, one will turn traditional papercut patterns into 3D printed ornaments, and another will weave bamboo into stylish modern lamps.
Visitors will even get the chance to try some of the skills themselves.
Your help would be greatly appreciated.
Since you are good at design and photography, could you help design the posters this week and take pictures during the event?
Please let me know if you are available.
Yours Li Ming
Dear John
I'm writing to tell you about a short play I'm planning.
based on the classic Chinese novel Journey to the West. It tells how the monkey king and his companions overcome all kinds of difficulties on their journey to obtain the Buddhist scriptures.
The play will last about 20 minutes and be performed in English at our College Art Festival next month.
Knowing that you love Chinese culture and have acting experience, I sincerely invite you to join us and play the role of Ju Bajie, a funny but kind-hearted character.
Rehearsals will be held every Saturday afternoon.
Please let me know if you are interested.
Best wishes. Li Ming.
Dear Paul
I'm glad to offer some advice on your oral report.
First, choose a scientist whose story interests you, such as Zhang Hung, who invented the world's first instrument for detecting earthquakes.
Next, collect reliable information from library books and museum websites, focusing on the scientists' major achievements and their influence.
Then organize your report around one or two vivid stories rather than a long list of facts, and use pictures or models to make it more engaging.
Finally, rehearse several times so that you can speak fluently and confidently.
I hope these tips help.
Good luck with your report.
Yours Li Ming
Dear Jack
I'm writing to share my plan for our survey on the protection of old houses in the ancient town.
I suggest we spend the first weekend of next month there.
On Saturday, we could photograph the old houses and record their current condition.
On Sunday, we could interview local residents and officials to learn what has been done to protect these buildings and what problems remain.
After that, we could write up a joint report with our suggestions.
What do you think of this plan?
Please let me know if you have any better ideas.
Best regards. Li Meng.
Research assistant wanted
Professor Smith from the School of Physical Education is looking for a student assistant for a research project on campus sports activities, which will run from March to June.
The assistant will be responsible for distributing and collecting questionnaires, interviewing students about their exercise habits and organizing the data collected.
The job requires about eight hours a week, and a monthly allowance will be provided.
Applicants should be full-time students with a keen interest in sports.
Good communication skills and a basic knowledge of statistical software are also required.
Those interested are welcome to send a brief CV to Professor Smith's office. Room 305, Sports Building. Before March 1st,
Li Meng
Dear David
I'm glad you asked for my advice.
In my opinion, the robot show would be the better choice for you.
To begin with, as a big fan of science and technology, you will find it truly fascinating.
Engineers from leading companies will demonstrate their latest robots, and visitors can even interact with some of them.
Moreover, you once told me that you were thinking of majoring in artificial intelligence. So the show may well give you some inspiration.
Besides, art exhibitions are held quite often in our city, whereas a robot show like this is a rare opportunity.
I hope you enjoy the show and have a great Sunday.
Yours Li Ming
Dear international students
I am writing to tell you about our campus food festival, which will be held in the Central Square from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. next Saturday.
More than 30 stalls will offer a wide variety of dishes, from spicy Sichuan noodles to sweet Cantonese desserts.
You can also learn to make dumplings with local students and enjoy live music while you eat.
We warmly invite you to join us.
You are also welcome to bring a dish from your home country to share with everyone.
If you are interested, please sign up at the Student Union Office by Wednesday.
We look forward to seeing you there.
Sincerely yours, Li Ming.
Dear Emma
Congratulations on your graduation.
I'm delighted to hear that you plan to work in China.
Here are a few suggestions.
First it would be wise to improve your Chinese, as even basic language skills will make both job hunting and daily life much easier.
Second, think carefully about which city suits you best.
Big cities like Shanghai and Shenzhen offer more opportunities, but living costs there are much higher.
Third, begin your search on job websites and at career fairs for foreigners, and be sure to check the work visa requirements in advance.
I hope you find an ideal job soon.
If you need any help, just let me know.
Best wishes. Li Ming.
Dear Jack
I'm writing to invite you to an online meeting on traditional Chinese festivals, which I am organizing for international students.
The meeting will be held via Tencent meeting from 7 to 9 p.m. next Friday.
First, two professors from the history department will give short talks on the origins and customs of major festivals.
After that, everyone will be welcome to talk about festivals in their own countries.
Since you are so interested in Chinese culture, I'm sure you will enjoy it.
I will send you the meeting ID and password the day before.
Please let me know by Wednesday whether you can attend.
Yours Li Ming
